The Case for Lawful Access: Why Absolute Encryption Endangers Public Safety

A Necessary Recalibration of Priorities

In democratic societies, no right has ever been treated as absolute. Freedom of speech does not protect incitement to violence. The right to bear arms does not extend to private ownership of nuclear weapons. Property rights yield to lawful search warrants. Yet somehow, in the digital realm, a radical and historically unprecedented idea has taken root: that private communications should be placed in a mathematical vault so secure that no lawful authority—no judge, no court, no democratic institution—can access them, even with probable cause and due process. This position is untenable, and governments are right to consider mandating lawful access mechanisms in consumer encrypted communications.

The Warrant-Proof Space Problem

The core argument is straightforward. For centuries, democratic societies have maintained a careful balance: citizens enjoy robust privacy protections, but those protections yield when an independent judiciary determines that sufficient cause exists to authorize a search. End-to-end encryption, as currently implemented by major technology companies, shatters this balance entirely. It creates what former FBI Director James Comey called "warrant-proof spaces"—domains where even a perfectly lawful, constitutionally sound court order is rendered meaningless by technological design.

This is not a minor procedural inconvenience. It represents a fundamental restructuring of the relationship between democratic governance and individual autonomy, enacted not by legislatures or constitutional amendments, but by private technology companies making unilateral design decisions. No democratic polity ever voted to create spaces permanently beyond the reach of lawful authority. The encryption absolutists have effectively engineered a fait accompli, and then demanded that society bear the consequences.

The Human Cost of Going Dark

The consequences are not abstract. They are measured in human suffering.

Child sexual exploitation represents perhaps the most visceral illustration. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) has repeatedly warned that end-to-end encryption severely undermines the ability to detect and report child sexual abuse material (CSAM). When Meta announced plans to encrypt Facebook Messenger by default, NCMEC estimated it could lose millions of annual CSAM reports. These are not statistics—they represent real children being abused, whose abusers are shielded by encryption designed to protect the privacy of ordinary messaging. In 2022, technology companies reported over 32 million instances of CSAM. How many will go undetected in a fully encrypted ecosystem?

Terrorism continues to exploit encrypted platforms. The attackers responsible for numerous incidents across Europe and elsewhere coordinated through encrypted messaging services. Intelligence agencies across the Five Eyes alliance have consistently testified that encryption poses one of the most significant barriers to identifying and disrupting terror plots before they materialize. Every successful attack that could have been prevented represents a catastrophic failure—not of intelligence agencies, but of a system that allows terrorist coordination to be technologically impervious to lawful surveillance.

Organized crime, drug trafficking, and human trafficking networks have migrated enthusiastically to encrypted platforms precisely because they provide operational security superior to anything previously available. The takedown of EncroChat in 2020—a dedicated encrypted phone network used almost exclusively by criminals—resulted in over 1,000 arrests and the seizure of massive quantities of drugs, weapons, and criminal assets. This was only possible because authorities found a way to penetrate the encryption. The lesson is clear: when law enforcement can access criminal communications, it saves lives and dismantles criminal enterprises. When it cannot, those enterprises flourish.

The Fallacy of Absolute Security

Encryption advocates argue that any lawful access mechanism inherently weakens security for all users, creating vulnerabilities that malicious actors could exploit. This argument, while technically serious, is overstated and ultimately proves too much.

First, it assumes a binary between perfect security and no security. In reality, security exists on a spectrum, and every system already involves tradeoffs. Technology companies routinely maintain access to vast quantities of user data for their own commercial purposes. They build internal tools capable of scanning, analyzing, and processing communications at scale. The argument that building a carefully designed lawful access mechanism is technically impossible strains credibility when these same companies build enormously complex systems for advertising, content moderation, and platform integrity every day. The technical challenge is real but not insurmountable—it is a matter of engineering priorities and investment.

Second, leading cryptographers and security researchers have proposed various models for lawful access that do not require a single "golden key." Key escrow systems, client-side scanning, ghost protocol proposals, and multi-party threshold schemes all represent potential approaches. None is perfect, but the dismissal of every proposed solution by the technology industry should be viewed with appropriate skepticism. These companies have powerful commercial incentives to market absolute encryption as a feature and powerful institutional reasons to resist any obligation to cooperate with law enforcement. Their technical objections, while worth taking seriously, are not disinterested assessments.

Third, the "weakened security" argument proves too much because it logically extends to opposing any form of lawful access to anything. By the same reasoning, we should oppose all search warrants because they "weaken" physical security. We should oppose wiretap laws because they create interception capabilities. We should oppose bank reporting requirements because they create data vulnerabilities. Every mechanism of lawful access involves some degree of risk. Society has always judged that the risk is worth bearing because the alternative—total immunity from lawful investigation—is worse.

The Democratic Legitimacy Argument

Perhaps the most troubling aspect of the encryption debate is its anti-democratic character. Technology companies have arrogated to themselves the power to determine, through product design, the boundaries of government authority. This is a decision that belongs to democratic institutions.

When Apple, Meta, or Signal decide to implement end-to-end encryption without any lawful access mechanism, they are not merely making a technical decision. They are making a profound political and constitutional choice about the limits of state power—a choice that in any democratic society should be made by elected representatives, subject to judicial oversight and constitutional review. The encryption absolutist position effectively says: "We, the technology industry, have determined that no government, regardless of its democratic legitimacy, its judicial safeguards, or its constitutional framework, should be able to access these communications. This decision is final and not subject to democratic deliberation."

This is techno-libertarian overreach of the most dangerous kind. It subordinates democratic self-governance to the ideological preferences of Silicon Valley engineers and the commercial interests of technology corporations. Democratic societies have every right—indeed, an obligation—to assert that the rule of law extends to digital spaces just as it does to physical ones.

International Security and Geopolitical Realities

The encryption debate cannot be divorced from geopolitical realities. Nation-states face genuine security threats from foreign adversaries, terrorist organizations, and transnational criminal networks. Intelligence capabilities are not luxuries—they are essential instruments of national survival.

The argument that authoritarian regimes would exploit lawful access mechanisms is a serious concern but not a decisive one. Democratic nations already maintain legal frameworks for surveillance that are fundamentally different from authoritarian systems. The existence of lawful interception capabilities in telephone networks has not transformed Western democracies into police states. The same legal safeguards—judicial warrants, oversight committees, proportionality requirements, and independent review—can and should govern digital lawful access.

Moreover, the status quo is not strategically neutral. When Western technology companies provide unbreakable encryption to all users globally, they provide it equally to adversary intelligence services, terrorist organizations, and hostile non-state actors. The idealistic notion that strong encryption uniformly serves freedom is contradicted by the reality that it also serves those who would destroy freedom.

Answering the Civil Liberties Objection

Civil liberties advocates raise important concerns that deserve serious engagement, not dismissal. Privacy is a genuine and important right. Government surveillance powers can be and have been abused. These concerns, however, counsel in favor of strong oversight and robust legal safeguards—not in favor of making surveillance technically impossible regardless of circumstances.

The civil liberties framework that has served democratic societies for generations is built on a principle of conditional privacy: your privacy is protected unless and until a legitimate authority, operating under legal constraints, determines that specific grounds exist to intrude upon it. This framework has never guaranteed unconditional, absolute, technologically enforced immunity from all government access. Encryption absolutism does not preserve the traditional balance of civil liberties—it radically and unilaterally transforms it.

Furthermore, privacy is not the only civil liberty at stake. Victims of crime have rights. Children have a right to be protected from exploitation. Citizens have a right to security. The absolutist framing that pits "privacy" against "government surveillance" ignores the rights of victims and potential victims whose safety depends on effective law enforcement.

A Reasonable Path Forward

The call for lawful access is not a call for mass surveillance. It is not a call for abolishing privacy. It is a call for restoring the balance that has historically existed between individual privacy and the legitimate needs of law enforcement and national security, adapted for the digital age.

A reasonable lawful access framework would include:

  • Judicial authorization requirements, ensuring that access is only granted pursuant to warrants based on probable cause or equivalent legal standards
  • Strict purpose limitations, restricting the use of accessed communications to serious crimes and genuine national security threats
  • Independent oversight, including parliamentary committees, judicial review, and independent inspectors general
  • Transparency reporting, requiring regular public accounting of the frequency and nature of lawful access requests
  • Technical standards, developed collaboratively between government, industry, and independent security researchers, to minimize security risks while enabling lawful access
  • Severe penalties for unauthorized access or misuse of lawful access capabilities

Such a framework is not utopian—it mirrors existing frameworks for wiretapping, financial surveillance, and physical searches that have operated for decades in democratic societies without producing the dystopian outcomes that critics predict.

Conclusion

The question before democratic societies is not whether privacy matters—it does, enormously. The question is whether private technology companies should be permitted to create spaces that are permanently, irrevocably beyond the reach of democratic governance and the rule of law. The answer should be no.

Absolute end-to-end encryption without lawful access provisions is not a natural right. It is a recent technological development, driven by commercial interests and ideological commitments, that has created an unprecedented challenge to public safety. Democratic societies have both the right and the responsibility to insist that the rule of law must be technically enforceable in digital spaces, just as it is in physical ones. The cost of inaction is measured in exploited children, successful terrorist attacks, and thriving criminal enterprises. That cost is too high to bear in the name of an absolute that no democratic society has ever recognized.

The time has come to move beyond the false binary of "perfect encryption or no security" and build a framework that honors both privacy and public safety. Our children, our communities, and our democratic institutions deserve nothing less.

The Case for Lawful Access: A Speech

We do not allow banks to build vaults that cannot be opened pursuant to court order. We do not allow landlords to construct apartments that cannot be entered with a warrant. We do not permit hospitals to create records that are permanently beyond subpoena. The drug traffickers whose logistics now run through encrypted channels. The human traffickers, the organized crime syndicates, the foreign agents operating on our soil.

The telephone system operated for a century with lawful intercept capabilities, and it was not destroyed by that capability. Society did not collapse. Democracy did not fall.

We are told that authoritarian governments will exploit any mechanism we create. But let us be clear-eyed: authoritarian governments do not need backdoors. They compel access through force, they seize devices, they imprison engineers. The notion that American lawful access policy is the thin line protecting dissidents in authoritarian states is, frankly, flattering to ourselves but detached from reality. Those regimes will do what they will do regardless. Our question—the only question before us—is whether our democratic institutions, with our constitutional safeguards, with our independent judiciary, will retain the ability to enforce our laws.
